assumptions: The family installer will permit a lawful opt-in pilot without transferring or improperly repurposing homeowner data.
The founder can commit approximately 15 hours weekly while retaining employment and can outsource operational work as adoption grows.
At least some inspection, warranty, inverter, battery, or repair events can support repeat revenue even if universal annual PV maintenance does not.
No signed customer, distributor, data-access, or technician-capacity commitment exists beyond the described informal relationship.
evidence_needed_for_higher_score: A paid, consent-compliant pilot across a meaningful installed-base cohort showing homeowner offer rate, conversion, average service revenue, repeat frequency, fulfillment rate, refunds, installer retention, onboarding labor, fully loaded contribution margin, and CAC payback; followed by several unaffiliated signed installers and at least one repeatable distributor or direct-sales channel.

factors.name: Core insight
factors.rationale: A very large installed renewable-asset base and installers' weak post-installation monetization create a plausible renewal opportunity. The insight is weakened because the evidence supports episodic inspections and repairs more strongly than a recurring annual-maintenance need.

factors.name: Customer pain and willingness to pay
factors.rationale: Publicly priced PV inspection services establish a real paid event, and installers could value incremental repeat revenue. However, homeowner urgency, annual-plan conversion, installer price acceptance, and repeat behavior are unvalidated, while authoritative guidance that PV modules require little maintenance is materially adverse.

factors.name: Business model and economics
factors.rationale: Prepaid platform fees plus revenue share offer favorable cash conversion and some alignment with customer results. The proposed margins, CAC, payback, retention, onboarding burden, service frequency, and owner earnings are assumptions; 20-40 onboarding hours and uncertain service demand could make a relatively low monthly fee unattractive.

factors.name: Market and beachhead
factors.rationale: Poland's more than 1.6 million renewable microinstallations provide a substantial underlying asset base, and installers with 500-5,000 systems form a specific, reachable beachhead. The economically serviceable market may be much smaller because asset count does not establish maintenance frequency or spending.

factors.name: Competitive position and domination potential
factors.rationale: A specialized, revenue-linked managed offering could outperform generic reminder tools for smaller installers. Yet solar CRMs already offer service history, scheduling, automated touchpoints, payments, and portals, and there is no exclusive channel or owned control point supporting segment domination.

factors.name: Expansion potential
factors.rationale: A successful renewal workflow could extend into batteries, heat pumps, EV chargers, warranties, inspections, repairs, financing, and additional European installer markets. Those adjacencies become valuable only if the initial service cadence and installer distribution are proven.

factors.name: Defensibility and durability
factors.rationale: Campaign, payment, and service-record workflows are readily reproducible or bundleable by CRMs, distributors, and equipment vendors. Permissioned benchmark data might compound, but data access, pooling rights, optimization lift, proprietary mechanisms, and exclusive contracts are all unproven.

factors.name: Strength of advantage
factors.rationale: A managed revenue rail may be more outcome-oriented and convenient than standalone reminders, particularly for installers lacking service operations. No evidence yet shows a decisive improvement in conversion, revenue, workflow cost, or customer experience versus configurable CRM and payment products.

factors.name: Timing and momentum
factors.rationale: Poland's large accumulated PV base is reaching a stage where warranty administration, inverter issues, inspections, and repairs can matter, making post-installation monetization timely. Momentum is tempered by the low routine-maintenance profile of PV and the presence of capable software incumbents.

factors.name: Distribution
factors.rationale: The family installer relationship provides a credible, low-cost route to an opt-in pilot and matches the founder's regional access. It is nonexclusive, revocable, and does not confer homeowner-data rights; distributor referrals, repeatable installer acquisition, CAC, sales cycle, and close rates remain unverified.

factors.name: Execution and risks
factors.rationale: The founder's analytical skills, AI leverage, available capital, family-industry access, and ability to pilot part-time make initial execution feasible. Material risks include GDPR-compliant outreach, installer authorization, technician capacity, service quality, data cleaning, and dependence on partners the venture does not control.

highest_value_structural_change: Broaden the rail from annual PV maintenance to contractually embedded lifecycle revenue across batteries, heat pumps, warranties, mandatory electrical checks, monitoring alerts, and break-fix events, with opt-in captured at installation and multi-year installer agreements granting permissioned workflow and outcome-data rights.
main_structural_strength: The founder has an unusually practical, low-capital route to test a measurable post-installation revenue workflow through a relevant family installer while retaining the corporate job.
primary_score_limiter: The model depends on recurring homeowner service demand and installer willingness to share revenue, but the strongest available evidence indicates low routine PV maintenance needs and provides no observed conversion or fully loaded unit economics.
strongest_disconfirming_evidence: The US Department of Energy states that photovoltaic modules have no moving parts and require very little maintenance, undermining the assumed annual service cadence, homeowner urgency, recurring revenue pool, and consequently the platform's retention and revenue-share economics.
